intro: A carpenter checks that a wall is square by measuring 3 feet along one edge, 4 feet along the other, and making sure the diagonal is exactly 5 feet. A bridge engineer bolts steel into triangles because a triangle cannot change shape without breaking a bar. A county board wants a fire station the same distance from three towns. Each of these people is relying on a fact about shapes that is not just usually true but always true, and this unit is about how we know.

The unit begins with the rules of reasoning: what a definition is, what you are allowed to assume, and how a chain of if-then statements turns into a proof that no one can argue with. Then it uses those rules on real questions. When are two shapes truly the same? Which three measurements pin down a triangle, and which three do not? Where do the special lines of a triangle cross, and why do they cross at all?

By the end you will be able to write a proof in two columns, in a paragraph or as a flow chart, move a figure on a coordinate grid with a rule, prove two triangles congruent with SSS, SAS, ASA or AAS, and locate the circumcenter, incenter and centroid of any triangle. You will also be able to say, in every case, exactly why the answer is right.
bigQuestion: How can a few accepted rules and careful reasoning prove facts about shapes that are true every time, everywhere?

timeline.t: Thales of Miletus is credited with the first geometric proofs, including that the base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal
Euclid's Elements organizes geometry into definitions, postulates and proofs, one theorem resting on the last
The first printed edition of the Elements appears in Venice, and the book becomes a standard school text for centuries
René Descartes links algebra and geometry with coordinates, making coordinate proofs possible
Giovanni Saccheri tries to prove Euclid's fifth postulate by contradiction and unknowingly explores a new geometry
Nikolai Lobachevsky publishes a geometry in which the parallel postulate is false, and nothing contradicts itself
Pierre Wantzel proves that trisecting a general angle with compass and straightedge is impossible
Abraham Lincoln of Springfield, Illinois, writes that he nearly mastered six books of Euclid to learn what it means to demonstrate
Felix Klein describes geometry as the study of what transformations leave unchanged, the view behind rigid motions
David Hilbert publishes a complete, careful set of axioms for Euclidean geometry, filling gaps Euclid left
Albert Einstein's general relativity describes gravity using curved, non-Euclidean geometry
The Common Core standards, adopted in Illinois, define congruence through rigid motions, the approach this unit follows

words.d: a statement accepted as true without proof; a starting rule of geometry
a statement that has been proved from postulates, definitions and earlier theorems
one example that fits the hypothesis but breaks the conclusion, proving a conjecture false
the statement formed by swapping and negating both parts of a conditional; it always matches the original's truth
a line that crosses two or more other lines, creating corresponding and alternate interior angles
a translation, reflection or rotation; a transformation that preserves distances and angles
two figures are congruent if a sequence of rigid motions maps one exactly onto the other
the angle between two given sides of a triangle; needed for the SAS criterion
corresponding parts of congruent triangles are congruent; used after triangles are proved congruent
the point where the perpendicular bisectors of a triangle meet; equidistant from the three vertices
the point where the angle bisectors of a triangle meet; equidistant from the three sides
the point where the medians of a triangle meet; two thirds of the way from each vertex, and the balance point

test.q: Point B is between A and C. AB = x + 4, BC = 2x − 1 and AC = 21. What is AB?
What is the converse of 'If two lines are perpendicular, then they form right angles'?
choices: If two lines are not perpendicular, then they do not form right angles
If two lines do not form right angles, then they are not perpendicular
If two lines form right angles, then they are perpendicular
Two lines are perpendicular only if they are parallel
test.why: The converse swaps the hypothesis and the conclusion without negating either one.

test.q: Which figure is a counterexample to 'Every quadrilateral with four congruent sides is a square'?
choices: a rectangle that is 3 by 5
a trapezoid
a square with side 4
a rhombus with a 60° angle
test.why: A rhombus has four congruent sides, but with a 60° angle it is not a square. The rectangle does not even have four congruent sides.

test.q: Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. Alternate interior angles measure (4x − 5)° and (2x + 31)°. What is the measure of each angle?
test.why: Alternate interior angles are congruent: 4x − 5 = 2x + 31, so x = 18 and each angle is 4(18) − 5 = 67°. The 18 is only x.

test.q: The proof that vertical angles are congruent depends mainly on which fact?
choices: angles in a linear pair are supplementary
corresponding angles are congruent
the angles of a triangle add to 180°
all right angles are congruent
test.why: Each vertical angle forms a linear pair with the same angle, so both equal 180° minus that angle.

test.q: What is the image of (−3, 7) after a 180° rotation about the origin?
test.why: A 180° rotation changes the sign of both coordinates: (−3, 7) becomes (3, −7).

test.q: What is the image of (5, 2) after a reflection across the y-axis?
test.why: Reflecting across the y-axis changes the sign of x and keeps y: (5, 2) becomes (−5, 2).

test.q: Two triangles have two pairs of congruent angles and a pair of congruent sides that are not between those angles. Which criterion applies?
choices: ASA
AAS
SAS
SSA
test.why: Two angles and a non-included side is AAS. It works because the third angle is forced by the angle sum.

test.q: Why is SSA not a valid congruence criterion?
choices: Because it uses too few parts
Because angles cannot be measured exactly
Because the side opposite the given angle can swing into two different positions, making two triangles
Because it only works for equilateral triangles
test.why: With two sides and a non-included angle, the second side can cross the opposite ray in two places, so two different triangles can share those measurements.

test.q: In parallelogram ABCD, angle A = (3x + 10)° and angle C = (5x − 30)°. What is the measure of angle B?
test.why: Opposite angles are congruent: 3x + 10 = 5x − 30, so x = 20 and angle A = 70°. Angle B is consecutive to A, so it measures 180 − 70 = 110°.

test.q: A triangle's angles measure 3x, 4x and 5x. What is the largest angle?
test.why: 3x + 4x + 5x = 12x = 180, so x = 15. The largest angle is 5(15) = 75°.

test.q: The base angles of an isosceles triangle measure (3x + 8)° and (5x − 14)°. What is the vertex angle?
test.why: Base angles are congruent: 3x + 8 = 5x − 14, so x = 11 and each base angle is 41°. The vertex angle is 180 − 41 − 41 = 98°.

test.q: G is the centroid of a triangle, and AD is a median. If GD = 7, what is the length of AD?
test.why: GD is one third of the median, so AD = 3 × 7 = 21. AG would be 14.

test.q: Two sides of a triangle measure 6 and 13. Which of these could be the third side?
test.why: The third side must be greater than 13 − 6 = 7 and less than 13 + 6 = 19, not including the endpoints. Only 8 fits.

test.q: A right triangle has vertices (0, 0), (0, 8) and (6, 0), with the right angle at the origin. Where is its circumcenter?
test.why: The circumcenter of a right triangle is the midpoint of the hypotenuse from (0, 8) to (6, 0): (3, 4). It is 5 units from every vertex. The point (2, 8/3) is the centroid.

write.prompt: Three towns sit at (0, 0), (12, 0) and (0, 10) on a map with units in miles. Find the point that is the same distance from all three towns, show every calculation, and explain why the three perpendicular bisectors must meet at one point. Then explain, using a triangle center, where you would put a station that is instead equally close to the three roads joining the towns.
tips: State your final point clearly and say which triangle center it is.
Show each step: the midpoint of each side, the equation of each perpendicular bisector, and where they cross.
Check your answer with the distance formula to all three towns.
Explain in a sentence why any point on a perpendicular bisector is equidistant from the segment's endpoints.
Name the second center, say which segments locate it, and explain why it is always inside the triangle.
